Summary

  1. The U.S.-China trade truce is likely to survive past January 10. But chip export controls run on a separate track, so the pressure on South Korean chipmakers will remain even if the truce holds.
  2. If Miami produces a major announcement, it will mean Washington has agreed to pay the price. The first signal is whether, in early December, the U.S. announces a date for implementing its tariff cuts. If Xi Jinping attends in person, it will mean Washington has already paid.
  3. In Ukraine, a prisoner exchange is the most the G20 can deliver, and a deal with Iran is unlikely before the end of March. Whatever Trump achieves in Miami will center on U.S.-China issues.

What Clisa Geopolitics expects

1. The truce will hold past January 10. In none of the 72 runs did U.S.-China tariffs and China's rare-earth export controls all snap back at once; in only one did either side restore some of its measures. Clisa Geopolitics' published forecast also puts the chance that the truce is extended or replaced by a longer deal at 70%. The open question is not whether the truce ends, but how long it runs and what gets added to it.

2. If a major deal comes, Washington will pay first. In the simulations, every major deal, whether implementation of the "$30 billion for $30 billion" tariff cuts or a one-year extension, included the U.S. actually putting its tariff cuts into effect. In the runs that also covered whether Xi would come to the G20, China committed to attending and to a deal only after the U.S. had first set a date for implementing the tariff cuts and signaled it would hold off on new chip restrictions. So the first signal to watch in early December comes from Washington, not Beijing: whether the U.S. announces a date for implementing the tariff cuts.

3. If Xi comes to Miami in person, take it as a sign that Washington has already paid. Xi has already met Trump twice this year (a state visit to Washington in September and a three-way summit in Shenzhen in November). In the simulations, a U.S. invitation alone was never enough to bring him. Trump, by contrast, lost both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterms and will face a Democratic-controlled Congress from January 3. He is the one in a hurry. In Clisa Geopolitics' view, when the host who has set the stage is left waiting on a guest, it is the guest who sets the price of showing up. This matches the judgment in its November 18 feature, "Trump's last two years: a president in a hurry, strongmen who can wait" Read the feature.

4. However the truce is extended, chip export controls will not be lifted. In none of the 72 runs did the U.S. lift its existing controls, whether the export-licensing regime or the remote-access rule, which requires licenses for overseas data centers that provide advanced-chip computing to Chinese companies. What Washington put on the table went no further than letting already-licensed sales continue and holding off on new restrictions; the furthest any run went was delaying enforcement of the remote-access rule. The trade truce and chip controls run on separate tracks.

5. In Ukraine, the most the G20 can deliver is a prisoner exchange. In the 40 runs that included Russia and Ukraine, no ceasefire was reached before the end of March, and Putin never came to Miami. For Putin, a summit stage on American soil is leverage for extracting concessions in the Ukraine negotiations, so he had no reason to come without getting something in return The Russia-Ukraine War.

6. A deal with Iran is unlikely before the end of March. In the same 40 runs, no agreement was signed; outcomes swung between talks that produced no deal and renewed U.S. strikes. The sticking point was always the same: Iran would not budge on keeping enriched uranium on its own soil. Trump has put off his decision on resuming strikes until "after the new year," so January will be the turning point The Iran War and Hormuz.

What it means for South Korea

A one-year extension would ease U.S.-China tariff uncertainty for South Korean exporters through next year; a short extension of three to seven months would bring the same uncertainty back next spring. And because chip controls run on a separate track, the pressure on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, over approvals to ship equipment to their plants in China and over chip exports to China, will remain even if the truce holds.

Whether Washington keeps the rule or delays it will test whether chips stay on a separate track.		January 19

Clisa Geopolitics will revise this outlook if the truce lapses on January 10 or either side reinstates measures; if Xi attends and a major deal emerges without Washington moving first; if the U.S. actually lifts existing chip export controls in exchange for a trade deal; or if a Ukraine ceasefire or an Iran deal is signed before the end of March.

How the experiment worked

AI models played the decision-makers of the United States (the president, Treasury secretary, trade representative and commerce secretary), China (the president, vice premier and commerce ministry), Russia, Ukraine, Europe, Iran (through mediators) and the Gulf states. Each side's goals were drawn solely from what its government has said and done in public. The inputs were limited to facts made public by November 22, 2026, and the models were not shown Clisa Geopolitics' published probabilities. Because the share of runs producing each outcome varied widely with the experiment's design, those shares are not treated as probabilities; only results that held under every design are presented as forecasts. Probabilities are left to Clisa Geopolitics' published forecasts Forecasts and Track Record.

What's next

After the Miami G20, Clisa Geopolitics plans to run the same experiment again and, before January 10, publish how the results have changed, then compare them with actual outcomes on January 10 and at the end of March.
